ideas.title: Night Golf
ideas.oneLiner: A turnkey night-golf package — glow gear, lit greens and an events playbook — sold B2B to Canadian courses so they can run fun, party-atmosphere evenings and unlock off-peak revenue.

market.why: Refined to Canada (owner's call). It's a healthy, growing market — ~2,047 golf course/club businesses, ~6M golfers, ~11M rounds posted in 2024, ~C$4.0B revenue growing at ~4.5% CAGR with record rounds in 2025, and youth/female participation as a tailwind. But it's roughly one-eighth the course count of the US, so the B2B addressable base (courses as customers) is modest in absolute terms.

entry.why: Low barriers on the lean events/kit path — commodity-sourceable glow gear, cheap portable LED kit, no regulation. Being first with a turnkey B2B offering in Canada (the scaled US incumbent isn't operating here) makes entry easier, not harder.

cost.why: Cheap to first revenue on the events/kit path: a few thousand dollars of portable LED gear plus glow inventory books paid event nights quickly. Caveat: Canada's short season concentrates revenue into ~5–6 warm months, so annual economics hinge on that window.

saturation.why: Much better than the US read. The scaled incumbent (Glow Vibe Golf, 36 US states) shows no Canadian presence, and Canada has only scattered DIY course events (e.g. NINE Golf in Belleville, Heritage Creek, a par-3 in Ottawa) rather than a turnkey B2B provider. The niche looks open — not empty, but genuinely under-served.

moat.why: Still structurally weak — commodity gear, replicable events — but a Canadian first-mover position, exclusive course contracts/territories, and a recurring-consumables kit could build a modest, defensible base before US operators expand north.

margins.why: Mixed. Commodity consumables (glow balls, markers) are low-margin but recurring; staffed experiences and event bookings carry higher service margins. Blended margin is moderate and scales through a kit/franchise model rather than manufacturing.

founderFit.why: Confirmed by the owner: the team has NO existing golf-course relationships, which is the key drag on B2B adoption by conservative operators. Offsetting positives — the team is based in the target market (Canada), with overseas sourcing for low-cost gear, strong experiential-marketing and product-engineering skills, and B2B/finance capability for selling to operators.

risk.why: Mixed after refinement. Lower: no scaled competitor in Canada. Higher: a smaller market, no course relationships to open doors, and pronounced seasonality — Canada's short, cold golf season squeezes outdoor night play into a few months. Capital-at-risk stays low on the lean path, so downside is contained.

businessCase.summary: Refined per the owner: a turnkey night-golf offering — event nights plus a self-run 'night-golf-in-a-box' kit — sold B2B to Canadian golf courses so they can monetise otherwise-dead evening hours. The commodity glow-ball manufacturing path is explicitly out. Canada is the target because the scaled US incumbent (Glow Vibe Golf) isn't here — genuine first-mover whitespace — though it's a smaller market with a much shorter season and the team has no course relationships yet.
businessCase.customer: The paying customer is the Canadian golf-course / driving-range operator (B2B) — ~2,047 facilities, especially public, municipal and resort courses chasing off-peak and event revenue. The end users are social golfers, corporate outings and charity fundraisers, families, and the growing youth/female segments driving Canadian golf's growth.
businessCase.market: Canada: ~2,047 course/club businesses, ~6M golfers, ~11M rounds posted in 2024 and record rounds in 2025, ~C$4.0B industry revenue at ~4.5% CAGR. Smaller than the US but healthy and growing. The turnkey night-golf niche is under-served — only scattered DIY course events exist and no scaled turnkey B2B provider — so there's real first-mover room.
businessCase.model: Pure B2B: (1) turnkey glow event nights sold to courses per-event; (2) a 'night-golf-in-a-box' kit sold or leased so courses self-run events, generating upfront hardware plus recurring consumables (glow balls, markers, cart lights); (3) recurring replenishment revenue. Gear sourced overseas for a cost advantage. Explicitly NOT manufacturing/selling balls as a commodity.
businessCase.goToMarket: The team has no course relationships, so job one is building them — start local (the team is Canada-based), landing a few public/municipal or resort courses with paid pilot nights, then converting them to a recurring kit + consumables relationship. Lean on shareable experiential/social content and high-value corporate & charity bookings. Move first, before US operators expand north.
businessCase.costs: Lean path is cheap: a few thousand dollars of portable LED gear and glow inventory (overseas-sourced) to run the first events; ongoing costs are inventory, event staffing and logistics. The short Canadian season is the real economic constraint — plan for concentrated summer revenue and consider shoulder-season or indoor/simulator angles to smooth it.
businessCase.risks: A smaller market; pronounced seasonality (short, cold Canadian golf season); no existing course relationships to open doors; weak structural moat; and the possibility that a US incumbent expands into Canada. The upside is that the niche is currently open and capital-at-risk is low.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Build the first course relationships — the biggest gap. 2) Run 2–3 paid pilot nights at local Canadian courses to test willingness-to-pay and rebooking. 3) Decide the lead model (staffed events vs sell/lease kit) and nail the unit economics. 4) Lock an overseas-sourced gear cost advantage. 5) Work through the short-season economics (shoulder/indoor options).

clarifyingQuestions: Given Canada's short golf season, how does the business sustain year-round — shoulder-season formats, indoor/simulator play, or a southern/US expansion later?
What's the beachhead — which region and course type do we land first, and how do we win it with no existing relationships?
Which is the lead revenue model — staffed event nights, or selling/leasing the self-run kit + consumables — and what are the unit economics of each?
